Amylase. The carbohydrate-digesting enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of glycosidic bonds in starch and related polysaccharides, breaking them into smaller sugars like maltose and glucose. Amylase is secreted in saliva and pancreatic juice, which means it initiates carbohydrate digestion in the mouth and continues the work in the small intestine. The enzyme catalyzes hydrolysis of alpha-one-four-glycosidic bonds in starch. Two main types exist: alpha-amylase, which cleaves internal bonds through random cleavage, and beta-amylase, which cleaves from the ends, producing maltose. Salivary glands produce salivary amylase while the pancreas produces pancreatic amylase. Both are secreted into saliva and the small intestine. The process initially produces dextrins, then maltose and glucose, with further hydrolysis occurring via brush-border enzymes. The enzyme requires calcium ion as a cofactor for activity. Amylase is moderately fast, and starch digestion begins immediately in the mouth, though the residence time there is short. Amylase exemplifies dietary enzyme adaptation. Herbivores and omnivores rely on it to break down the enormous amounts of starch in plant foods, releasing glucose for energy. Elevated plasma amylase is a clinical marker of pancreatic disease. Different organisms have evolved varying numbers of amylase genes reflecting their starch consumption, and humans with historically high-starch diets show adaptations in amylase gene expression.
